uncited: Tetrahedralization Schemes define how a cubic voxel cell is decomposed into tetrahedra to facilitate isosurface extraction, addressing the topological ambiguities and artifacts inherent in standard cube-based methods like Marching Cubes.

Unlike sibling methods that may use fixed lookup tables or specific lattice constraints, this family focuses on the geometric partitioning strategy itself—determining vertex counts, tetrahedron shapes, and neighbor dependencies.

It sets itself apart by offering alternatives to the standard 5-tetrahedron or 6-tetrahedron decompositions, such as schemes using 12 or 24 tetrahedra, or those based on non-cubic lattices like BCC or Diamond, to improve surface smoothness or reduce lookup table memory.
The core mechanism involves replacing the standard cubic voxel with a set of non-overlapping tetrahedra that fill the same volume.
For each tetrahedron, the scalar field values at its four vertices are used to determine the intersection with an isosurface threshold $T$.
The algorithm checks the sign of $(S_i - T)$ for each vertex $i$.
where $V_1, V_2$ are the vertex positions and $S_1, S_2$ are their scalar values.
The collection of these intersection points forms the vertices of the output triangle mesh.

The specific scheme dictates the connectivity of these tetrahedra, whether new "fabricated" points (like cell centers) are introduced, and how adjacent cells share boundaries to ensure a manifold mesh.
It tiles cells such that odd/even position sums determine orientation, ensuring near cells use consistent diagonals.
The need for tetrahedralization arose from the topological ambiguities in Marching Cubes, where certain configurations could produce non-manifold surfaces or artifacts.
